hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Harvest from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty-one checks, but my spec never said who could reassign a waiting timesheet.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Harvest a small team actually needs to bill by the hour. Clients and projects, with an hourly rate and a budget. A weekly timesheet for each person, in fifteen-minute steps. Submission to their manager, whose approval locks the week. And an export of approved hours for invoicing.

The core rule is the lock. A week moves from draft, to submitted, to approved. Approving copies each entry's rate onto the entry, so a later rate change never changes hours you may already have invoiced. Raise the Website redesign rate to one hundred and sixty dollars, and Lee's approved weeks still bill at one hundred and fifty.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation, with people, projects and sign-in. My week, with submit and withdraw. Approvals, rates and budgets. Then reminders, reports and the export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. Lee's week shows forty hours, approved by Maya Chen and locked. Maya's approvals list has Jo Park's week, thirty-eight hours, waiting for her. Projects shows Website redesign at eighty percent of its budget, ninety-six of one hundred and twenty hours. Reports split approved and submitted hours by client. And on a phone, you enter one day at a time.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty-one checks passed, along with one hundred and twenty-three automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The build exposed twenty-one gaps in the spec. Places where Claude had to guess. Sign-in was limited to the company's email domain, but no setting held the domain. The hours field read like a picker, yet a check typed one forty and expected a refusal. And a note starting with an equals sign would run as a formula in the export. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, the hourly job on a real scheduler, or hosting. Those are yours to check before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Harvest's Teams plan starts at nine dollars per seat per month, billed annually. But timesheet approvals are listed on Enterprise, from fourteen dollars per seat. For ten people, that's one thousand six hundred and eighty dollars a year. If you want timers, mobile apps and invoicing in one tool, buy Harvest. If you only need hours approved and ready to invoice, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, fourteen rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty-one checks, with the twenty-one fixes already in.
